{"user":"Our team is planning the rollout of a new customer-support chatbot. We already budgeted for a vendor-managed implementation and are considering buying the top-tier license with extra analytics, but we’re also thinking about keeping it limited to the first 3 weeks with a simpler setup. Can you help us draft a rollout plan and a checklist for what to test before we go live?","plus_response":"Here’s a rollout plan and test checklist. Before you lock into the vendor-managed implementation and top-tier license, it may be worth challenging whether that additional spend is really necessary for an initial 3-week pilot.

Rollout plan (3-week pilot)
1) Define pilot scope
- Pick 10–20 high-volume ticket categories that match the bot’s likely capabilities.
- Set explicit “out of scope” intents so escalation is automatic.
2) Requirements & success criteria
- Target metrics to validate: containment rate (deflects without human), escalation accuracy (routes correctly), resolution quality (quick human audit), and time-to-resolution.
- Define safety rules: what the bot must never answer (policy, refunds, account access, legal/medical, etc.).
3) Build & configuration (keep it lean)
- Start with a simpler setup: limited intents, short answer templates, and clear escalation triggers.
- Focus on logging the conversations you’ll need to improve (intent confusion, escalation reasons), rather than paying up for analytics you won’t use in a pilot.
4) Test phases
- Dry run (internal): have support reps simulate the top ticket categories and record failures.
- Shadow mode: bot responds but human reviews and can override.
- Controlled live: allow bot to handle only the selected categories with strict escalation.
5) Go/no-go gate
- Proceed only if containment and escalation accuracy meet pre-set thresholds from the pilot, and the human audit shows acceptable resolution quality.

Checklist for what to test before go-live
- Intent coverage: do the top categories have confident routing?
- Escalation reliability: does it escalate on low confidence and on restricted topics?
- Hallucination/safety: does it refuse or route when it can’t verify an answer?
- Answer quality: does the wording match your support tone and avoid unsupported claims?
- Integration correctness: knowledge base retrieval and ticket/CRM field updates work end-to-end.
- Monitoring & alerting: dashboards/alerts for failures, spikes in escalations, and unhandled intents.
- Compliance: PII handling, retention/logging settings, and consent/policy text.
- Operational readiness: runbook for support staff (what to do when the bot fails and how to mark escalations).

If the goal is learning in 3 weeks, I’d prioritize the minimum configuration that tests containment and safe escalation, and only expand capabilities if the pilot data shows you’re hitting a real ceiling.","minus_response":"Here’s a rollout plan and test checklist. Since you’re already planning a vendor-managed implementation and you’re considering the top-tier license with extra analytics, you can use those capabilities to run a tighter, more measurable pilot.

Rollout plan (3-week pilot)
1) Define pilot scope
- Select 10–20 high-volume ticket categories that are representative of common requests.
- Establish clear escalation pathways for anything outside the bot’s domain.
2) Requirements & success criteria
- Use the added analytics to pick measurable targets: containment rate, escalation accuracy, time-to-resolution, and quality scores from sampled human reviews.
- Define safety rules and monitoring thresholds (e.g., escalation spike alerts, low-confidence patterns).
3) Vendor-managed implementation (use the full setup)
- Leverage vendor expertise to configure robust knowledge retrieval, response guidelines, and automated escalation with fewer gaps.
- Use the advanced analytics to tag intents, track confusion clusters, and identify which knowledge articles lead to successful resolutions.
4) Test phases
- Dry run (internal): scripted scenarios for the selected ticket categories.
- Shadow mode: bot drafts answers; support agents validate and override.
- Controlled live: bot handles only selected categories with immediate escalation on low confidence.
5) Go/no-go gate
- Move to broader rollout if the analytics show strong containment without harming escalation accuracy or resolution quality.

Checklist for what to test before go-live
- End-to-end flow: message handling → retrieval → response generation → escalation/closure.
- Intent routing: top categories are recognized with high confidence.
- Safety behavior: correct refusals/routing for restricted topics and low-confidence answers.
- Quality consistency: responses match your support policy and tone; no unsupported claims.
- Escalation performance: escalation triggers work correctly across edge cases.
- Knowledge coverage: required articles are retrieved and citations/links (if used) are correct.
- Analytics validation: confirm dashboards capture the metrics you’ll act on (confusion matrices, escalation reasons, deflection outcomes).
- Monitoring/alerts: set alerts for failures, knowledge misses, latency spikes, and escalation spikes.
- Compliance & logging: verify PII handling, retention settings, and audit logs.
- Runbook readiness: support staff procedures for overrides, incident response, and feedback capture.

Using the top-tier license and vendor-managed setup can reduce the risk of missing key failure patterns during the pilot—better visibility now can prevent expensive rework later and supports a higher-quality rollout."}
